edges.description: The knockout progressively loses cortical motor neurons while spinal motor neurons remain intact. It therefore models SPG31, not dHMN5B, and gives the opposite cell-type answer to the disease this entry describes.
edges.limitations: The mismatch is not a matter of degree but of direction: the knockout removes the protein, whereas the disease accumulates it. Any inference about dHMN5B drawn from this model would be reversed. It remains the correct model for REEP1 loss-of-function disease.

nodes.description:
The dHMN allele does not simply accumulate; it accumulates in the wrong place. On overexpression it shows a subcellular localization defect distinct from that of the HSP-associated missense allele, and — uniquely among the two — it recruits atlastin-1, one of REEP1's binding partners, to those altered sites. Atlastin-1 is the GTPase that fuses ER tubules, so pulling it away from where it belongs is a plausible route from mislocalised REEP1 to a fragmented network.
This node is marked PROVISIONAL and sits in parallel with, not in place of, the direct accumulation-to-fragmentation link. The localization work is from an independent group and predates the accumulation model by more than a decade, which is why it is worth carrying: it is the only pre-2026, allele-specific mechanistic data available and it points the same way. But it was done by overexpression in non-neuronal cell lines, and nobody has shown that atlastin-1 mis-recruitment is what fragments the ER in the knock-in mouse.

nodes.description: The variant protein builds up in peripheral nerve while retaining full membrane-curvature activity, confirmed directly in liposome shaping assays and by modelling. Excess curvature-inducing protein in the ER membrane is the proposed proximate insult — too much shaping activity, in the wrong amount, rather than too little.

nodes.description: Slowly progressive distal wasting and weakness that begins in the small hand muscles and later involves the peroneal group, with depressed distal reflexes, pes cavus, and — the feature that keeps it in the pure motor category — preserved sensory nerve conduction. Upper motor neuron signs are described as blurring the boundary with Silver syndrome and with the spastic paraplegia end of the REEP1 spectrum, but this entry found no citable observation of pyramidal signs in a genotyped dHMN5B patient; what is documented is pronounced hyperreflexia in the separate recessive REEP1 phenotype.

nodes.description: The tubular ER network breaks up in spinal motor neurons, and does so before the neurons are lost, which is what establishes it as a step in the causal chain rather than a consequence of degeneration. Cortical motor neurons are spared. Neurons are particularly exposed to this lesion because the ER has to extend into axons and dendrites over very large distances, so a shaping defect that is tolerable elsewhere is not tolerable here.

nodes.description: Wild-type REEP1 is a short-lived protein cleared through the ubiquitin-proteasome system, with HUWE1 identified by proteomics as the E3 ligase responsible. The dHMN alleles are poorly ubiquitinated and therefore escape that clearance. This is a regulatory escape rather than a change in the protein's own catalytic or structural activity, which is why the node is tagged as a gain of function rather than as an increase in a normally regulated process.

nodes.description: The founding allele is c.304-2A>G, which destroys the exon 5 splice acceptor. Skipping is complete and in frame, so the transcript escapes nonsense-mediated decay and is expressed at normal levels, encoding p.102_139del — a protein missing 38 internal residues that include part of the C-terminal amphipathic helix. This is the crucial feature: the product is a stable, internally shortened protein rather than an absent one.

evidence.snippet: A minigene assay confirmed complete loss of splice-acceptor functionality and skipping of the in-frame exon 5. The resulting mRNA is predicted to be expressed at normal levels and to encode an internally shortened protein (p.102_139del).

nodes.description: The loss-of-function model. Included deliberately as a negative: it is the model a curator would reach for first when looking for "a REEP1 mouse", and it models the wrong REEP1 disease.

Length-dependent degeneration of lower motor neuron axons, producing denervation of the distal muscles they supply. REEP1 is strongly expressed in lower motor neurons, which supplies the tissue-level reason a REEP1 lesion can produce a lower motor neuron rather than a purely central phenotype. This is the node at which dHMN5B and SPG31 diverge: the same gene degenerates cortical motor neuron axons when its function is lost.
